paragraphs.heading: A mind with many trades
paragraphs.text: Leonardo da Vinci lived from 1452 to 1519 and was an Italian polymath, at home in many fields. Active in the High Renaissance, he was a painter and sculptor, an architect and engineer, a draughtsman, a scientist and a theorist. He is widely called a genius who embodied the Renaissance humanist ideal. Only his younger contemporary Michelangelo did as much to shape the course of European art.

paragraphs.heading: Childhood near Vinci
paragraphs.text: He was born in or near the Tuscan hill town of Vinci, about 35 kilometres from Florence. His parents were not married: his mother, Caterina, was a young peasant woman, and his father, Piero, was a successful notary. Both parents married other people the year after he was born. His schooling was basic and informal, covering reading, writing and mathematics, and little else is known for sure about his early years.

paragraphs.heading: Training with Verrocchio
paragraphs.text: In the mid-1460s the family moved to Florence. At about 14, Leonardo became a studio boy in the workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio, the city's leading painter and sculptor. He was an apprentice by 17 and trained for seven years. There he learned drawing, painting and sculpting, but also chemistry, metalwork, mechanics, plaster casting and woodwork.

paragraphs.heading: Few paintings, huge fame
paragraphs.text: Fewer than 25 major works are credited to him, and many of those were left unfinished. Even so, he made some of the most influential paintings in Western art. Many rank the Mona Lisa as the best-known painting on Earth, and The Last Supper is the most reproduced religious painting ever made. In 2017 Salvator Mundi, credited wholly or partly to him, sold for US$450.3 million, a record for a painting sold at public auction.

paragraphs.heading: Inventions on paper
paragraphs.text: His notebooks are full of drawings and notes on anatomy, astronomy, botany, map-making and more. In them he imagined flying machines, an armoured fighting vehicle, concentrated solar power and the double hull. Few of these designs were built in his lifetime, or could have been, since the science of metals and engineering was still young. He also made major discoveries in anatomy, optics and geology. He never published them, and they had little or no direct effect on later science.

paragraphs.heading: On the move
paragraphs.text: After starting out in Florence, Leonardo spent many years working for Ludovico Sforza in Milan. He later worked again in Florence and Milan and briefly in Rome, gathering many students and imitators. At the invitation of Francis I he moved to France for his last three years, and he died there in 1519.
